paragraphs.heading: Salt lovers
paragraphs.text: A halophile, from the Greek for salt-loving, is an extremophile that thrives where salt is concentrated. Most belong to the domain Archaea, but some are bacteria, and a few are eukaryotes such as the alga Dunaliella salina and the fungus Wallemia ichthyophaga. Several well-known species look red, thanks to carotenoid compounds, notably bacteriorhodopsin.

paragraphs.heading: Where they live
paragraphs.text: Halophiles live in water more than five times saltier than the ocean, including Utah's Great Salt Lake, Owens Lake in California, Lake Urmia in Iran, the Dead Sea and evaporation ponds. In salt lakes and salterns, the extreme halophiles tint the water and the sediments bright colors. Scientists also see them as possible models for life that might exist in the salty ocean under the surface of Jupiter's moon Europa.

paragraphs.heading: How much salt
paragraphs.text: Halophiles are graded by how much salt they handle: slight, moderate or extreme. Slight halophiles prefer 0.3 to 0.8 M salt (seawater is 0.6 M, or 3.5%), moderate ones 0.8 to 3.4 M, and extreme ones 3.4 to 5.1 M, which is 20 to 30%. True halophiles need sodium chloride to grow. Halotolerant organisms differ: they can grow in salty conditions but do not need salt.

paragraphs.heading: Keeping water in
paragraphs.text: Very salty water is a harsh home, and few organisms have adapted to it. Most halophiles spend energy keeping salt out of their cytoplasm so their proteins do not clump together. Salty surroundings also draw water out of the cell, so halophiles raise their internal osmolarity to stop it drying out. In the first strategy, used by most halophilic bacteria, some archaea, and yeasts, algae and fungi, the cell builds up organic compounds called compatible solutes, either made itself or taken in. The commonest include amino acids, sugars, polyols, betaines and ectoines.

paragraphs.heading: The potassium route
paragraphs.text: The second, more radical strategy is to take potassium (K⁺) ions into the cytoplasm. Only three groups do this: the archaeal family Halobacteriaceae, the bacterial order Halanaerobiales and the bacterium Salinibacter ruber. Since these are three separate lineages, the strategy most likely evolved more than once. It asks much more of the cell, because all its internal machinery, such as enzymes and structural proteins, must be adapted to high salt, while compatible solutes need little or no such change.

paragraphs.heading: Fragile specialists
paragraphs.text: The extreme halophiles called haloarchaea need at least 2 M salt and usually live in saturated brine, about 36% salt. Their cell machinery copes by carrying charged amino acids on its surface, which keeps water molecules held around it. They normally respire with oxygen, though so much salt limits how much oxygen is available. Most halophiles cannot survive away from their salty homes, and many are so fragile that in distilled water they burst at once from the change in osmotic conditions.

paragraphs.heading: Who is really there
paragraphs.text: In very salty waters, the haloarchaea, especially the family Halobacteriaceae, make up most of the prokaryotic population. Many genera have been grown from saltern crystalliser ponds, including Haloferax, Halococcus and Halobacterium. Newer PCR-based methods that target 16S rRNA genes in natural samples, though, suggest some of the easiest genera to grow may not matter much in the wild. Haloarcula, for example, often appears in isolation studies yet is estimated to be under 0.1% of the community.
